body: Italian licence plates have blue strips on both sides, and a uniquely short front plate. While Albanian plates also have two blue strips, only Italian plates have a short front plate.
Italian bollards are triangular, white with a black top, and have a red front reflector. These are identical to bollards found in Albania.
Italian roads often feature solid white outer lines with no middle line, a combination less common in other Mediterranean countries.
The Italian language features many double consonants and words usually end in a vowel. The word for street is 'via'.
Italy has a classic Mediterranean landscape with rolling agricultural hills and forested mountain valleys.
Italian architecture often consists of pastel-coloured stone houses with terracotta roofs and wooden shutters.
Italy frequently uses round concrete poles, which is uncommon for a Mediterranean country.
A small white sticker can often be found on wooden utility poles in Italy.
The most common poletops in Italy are concrete and shaped like a trident.
Finding double guardrails on the side of the road is very common in Italy.
Italian guardrails feature red front reflectors, which helps distinguish them from Spanish guardrails that use yellow reflectors.
Italian guardrails have a distinct ending where the rail becomes flatter and wider as it bends away from the road.
The back of road signs in Italy is very commonly black or dark grey.
Italian directional signs are blue with a white arrow and feature text written in all capital letters.
Directional signs for national roads are blue, while signs for divided highways (Autostrade) are green. Both have a border matching their respective color.
Italian kilometre markers are white squares with a Roman numeral above an Arabic numeral, where the Roman numeral indicates 100-meter intervals.
Italian road numbers start with SS (State), SR (Regional), or SP (Provincial), indicating the scope of the road's administration.
Italian chevrons feature white arrows on a black background, a design also seen in Spain, Greece, and Albania.
Italian street signs are typically white with a thin blue border and black text.
The Italian pedestrian sign has five stripes and shows a person with no belt.
Signs with the text "passo carrabile" are common in urban areas and indicate no parking. The name of the municipality (comune) is often found at the top.
Italy has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which is mounted lower and has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur with a small protrusion.
The first digit of Italian area codes generally follows a geographical pattern, increasing towards the east and then south.
Each Italian region has its own unique flag.
In the region of South Tyrol, you will find bilingual signs in both Italian and German.
Bilingual French and Italian signs are found in the Aosta Valley, with street signs often showing both 'via' and 'rue'.
The Po Valley (Padan Plain) is extremely flat and often has a noticeable haze in the coverage due to poor air quality.
The area around Bari in the southeast features many olive plantations, bright rock walls, and red-colored dirt.
The Alpine region in northern Italy is characterized by tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.
Sicily's landscape is typically arid and hilly with agriculture and rocky mountains.
Grey rocks sticking out of the ground are a common feature in Sardinia. While also seen in Sicily, Sardinia's landscape is typically less arid.
Cacti are most commonly found in the southern regions of Italy, including Sicily, Sardinia, and Apulia.
Citrus plantations are mainly found in eastern Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria.
Rice paddies are primarily located in the western and central Po Valley, and sometimes in Sardinia.
In and around Tuscany, buildings are often made of irregular, unpainted brown-grey bricks.
Alpine architecture, featuring large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, is found in the northern Alpine region.
Buildings in the Aosta Valley often feature grey, uneven bricks and have an Alpine appearance.
Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges are a common sight in northeastern Italy, especially in the Veneto region.
Houses in the Apulian region are typically light-colored with flat roofs, often resembling Middle Eastern architecture.
The unique cone-shaped roof, known as a trullo, is specific to the Itria Valley in southeastern Italy, particularly around Alberobello.
Near the Slovenian border, you can find bilingual signs in Italian and Slovene.
The Italian exclave of Campione d'Italia in Switzerland has unique coverage with a low camera, long antenna, and a flag.
Mount Etna, Europe's tallest volcano, is a prominent feature visible from afar in eastern Sicily.
The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen from the plains surrounding Naples.
The city of Venice is easily recognizable by the numerous canals that run through it.
The Plana del Fùcino is a small plain in central Italy surrounded by mountains, featuring a distinct north-to-south road grid.
The volcanic island of Pantelleria features dark volcanic rocks in its walls and houses, often covered in yellow lichen.
The Aeolian Islands are a volcanic archipelago north of Sicily, characterized by volcanic soil and rocks.
Salina in the Aeolian Islands is distinctive for its twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.
Vulcano is recognizable by its volcano with an almost white dirt stripe along the mountainside, visible from afar.
Favignana has a distinct north-south mountain range splitting the island, flat areas with rock walls like Bari, and is non-volcanic.
San Domino island has only overcast Generation 2 coverage, giving it a generally gloomy appearance.
